name: Avoid second order URL redirection to untrusted site
associatedValueName: Call stack from user input source down to the target method
description:
This quality rule uses CAST's data-flow engine to detect open redirect vulnerabilities originating from data previously stored in and read back from a database (second order). It traces data flows from database-read values (e.g., ResultSet.getString/getObject in Java, SqlDataReader.GetString/GetValue in .NET, or equivalent column-reading APIs) and terminate in a redirection statement (e.g., Response.Redirect, HttpServletResponse.sendRedirect, or equivalent APIs depending on the technology) without adequate sanitization in between.
A violation is raised whenever data read back from the database reaches a redirection call. This is a second-order vulnerability: the data was written to the database at some earlier point, potentially by an untrusted source (a prior user request, an import, another service), and is trusted implicitly once it comes back out of storage. Depending on how the redirection target is constructed, this may allow an attacker to redirect users to an arbitrary, potentially malicious, destination — or it may only affect a secondary parameter of an otherwise fixed destination (see below).
Only tainted data affecting the actual destination (scheme, host, or path) qualifies as CWE-601; tainted data confined to a query argument does not change the destination and is more accurately addressed as a CWE-116 (or similar injection) issue. This distinction is best resolved for simple string concatenation patterns, while more elaborate constructions (e.g., String.Format, intraprocedural constant propagation, StringBuilder) may call for additional manual review to confirm the classification.
output:
List all methods that make resource calls forged by database content

It provides the following information:
 - Method full name
 - Call stack from database source down to the target method.
rationale:
If an attacker can control the destination of a redirect, the application can be leveraged to send victims to an untrusted, malicious site while the initial request still points to the legitimate, trusted domain. This makes the attack much harder to detect than a traditional phishing link, since the URL displayed to the user (or shared in a phishing email) belongs to the trusted application.
Typical consequences include:
-Phishing: users are redirected to a fake login page designed to steal credentials or personal data.
-Malware distribution: users are redirected to a site hosting malicious payloads.
-Trust abuse / bypass of security controls: some applications or security tools whitelist redirects coming from a trusted domain; an open redirect can be used to bypass such controls or to defeat URL-reputation filters, as the initial link points to a legitimate domain.
-Reputation damage: the trusted application is used as a stepping stone for the attack, which can damage user trust in the application and its brand.

remediation:
Avoid using inputs to build redirect targets. If it is not possible:
-Input validation: implement strict whitelist validation allowing only known-good redirect destinations
-Path restriction: use only predefined, relative paths and reject any external/absolute URLs
-Destination mapping: map user input to predefined target URLs through configuration or a lookup table, rather than passing the URL directly
-Exact matching: validate destination hosts through strict, exact comparison rather than substring or prefix checks
alternativeName: Ensure you URL redirection always goes to trusted sites
